Greedy forward feature selection with spatially blocked inner folds

Source: R/feature-selection.R
select_features_forward.Rd

Selects predictors by repeatedly adding whichever candidate most improves a cross-validated score, stopping when the best candidate's improvement is no larger than the fold-to-fold noise in it (rule = "se", the default) or no larger than tol (rule = "tol"). The first variable has a baseline to beat with every learner, so the selection can be empty.

Usage

select_features_forward(
  train_sf,
  response_var,
  candidate_vars,
  fit_fn,
  k = 5,
  method = c("block_kfold", "random_kfold"),
  block_size = NULL,
  metric = c("RMSE", "MAE", "R2"),
  tol = 0,
  max_vars = NULL,
  max_fits = 5000L,
  seed = 123,
  quiet = FALSE,
  auto_range = FALSE,
  select_on = c("all", "split"),
  rule = c("se", "tol"),
  se_mult = 1,
  null_fn = NULL
)

Arguments

train_sf

Training data (sf).

response_var

Character(1).

candidate_vars

Character vector of predictors to choose among.

fit_fn

A function (train_sf, predictor_vars) returning a spatial_fit. The signature takes two arguments because selection has to refit with different predictor sets.

k

Inner fold count. Default 5.

method

Inner fold method. Default "block_kfold".

block_size

Passed to make_folds(); inherit the outer block size so inner and outer blocks are on the same spatial scale.

metric

Score to optimise: "RMSE", "MAE" (minimised) or "R2" (maximised). Default "RMSE".

tol

Minimum improvement of the pooled score required to accept a variable, in the units of metric. Default 0. It is a floor under both rules: with rule = "tol" it is the whole test, and with rule = "se" the per-fold test applies as well. The first variable is judged against a baseline with every learner; see The baseline for the first variable. Any single number is accepted: Inf leaves nothing selected, and -Inf puts no floor under a step.

max_vars

Optional cap on how many predictors to select.

max_fits

Abort if the sweep would exceed this many model fits. Default 5000.

seed

RNG seed. It governs both the inner fold construction and the cross-validation itself: it is forwarded to cv_spatial(seed = ), which draws one RNG stream per fold from it, so it also seeds the learner inside every fold. A stochastic fit_fn is therefore reproducible from this one value.

quiet

Logical; suppress this function's progress message()s. It does not silence R warnings, nor the package's console log echo (see spatialkit_quiet for that). Default FALSE.

auto_range

Logical. If TRUE and method is "block_kfold", the autocorrelation range is estimated from the response (detrended on the candidates) and used as the minimum block size of the inner folds, exactly as in make_folds(); block_size still applies as a floor. Default FALSE, which keeps the geometric blocks. Inner blocks smaller than the range let a candidate be selected for spatial proximity to the response rather than for predicting it, which is the same failure the random_kfold caution above exists to prevent, so the leakage warning make_folds() raises applies here with more force than usual.

select_on

"all" (default) runs the sweep on every row of train_sf. "split" runs it on one spatially blocked half, then fits the selected set on that half and scores it on the other: score_holdout is then the selected model's metric on rows whose response the sweep never read (the sweep's own score is not; see "The score is not a performance estimate"). It is one estimate from one region: the halves share a border with no buffer, so rows near it are still correlated with the selection half. Both halves come back in $split. See the "Post-selection inference" section of determine_optimal_levels for the trade: coverage for half the sample.

rule

How a step is judged. "se" (default) accepts the best candidate when its pooled gain exceeds tol and its mean per-fold gain exceeds se_mult standard errors of that mean; "tol" accepts any pooled gain above tol, the behaviour before this argument existed. See When a variable is accepted.

se_mult

Number of standard errors the mean per-fold gain must exceed under rule = "se". Default 1; 0 asks only that the mean per-fold gain be positive.

null_fn

Optional function (train_sf) returning a fitted model with no predictors, used as the baseline for the first variable when fit_fn cannot fit an empty predictor set. Default NULL: fit_fn(train_sf, character(0)) is tried, and the training-fold mean is used when that fails. The example builds one.

Value

A list of class "feature_selection" (so that plot.feature_selection() draws the selection path) with selected (the chosen predictors, in the order they were added; possibly none), score, score_holdout, history, params, split, baseline and fold_scores. score is the winning set's cross-validated metric at the final step: the selection-internal optimum, optimistically biased because it was chosen as the best of many (see the section above), and NA when nothing was selected. history is a data.frame with step, variable, score, n_pred, gain, fold_gain and fold_gain_se, holding every candidate evaluated at every step, and a step = 0 row named "<none>" giving the baseline, so the first variable's gain can be read off directly. gain is the candidate set's improvement in the pooled score over the set it was added to (the baseline at step 1), fold_gain the mean of the per-fold improvements and fold_gain_se its standard error: the three numbers the rule reads. fold_scores is a data.frame with step, variable, fold and score: the metric of every set in every fold. baseline is a list with type ("null model", "null_fn" or "fold mean"), score, path (the set the sweep reached), gain, fold_gain and fold_gain_se (that set against the baseline), kept (FALSE when the path did not beat a fold-mean baseline and selected is empty for that reason; NA when the path is empty) and first. first is NULL unless the baseline is the fold mean and a path of two or more variables was kept; it is then the test of the first variable, a list with variable; gain, fold_gain and fold_gain_se (the path against the path without that variable); rest, a list with vars, score, gain, fold_gain and fold_gain_se (the path without it, and that set against the baseline); dropped (TRUE when the variable was taken out: selected is then path[-1] and score is rest$score); and note, the verdict in words. The set scored for that test is not a step of the sweep, so it is not in history or fold_scores. Every set is scored on the same rows: those the null model's cross-validation predicted or, when the baseline is the fold mean, those any step-1 set predicted; params$n_scored counts them (a warning says so when that is fewer than all). n_pred is how many rows the set's cross-validation predicted. A set that left some of the scored rows unpredicted, because a fold failed for it, has score NA, with a warning naming it: scored on the rows it did predict it would be compared on fewer, usually easier, rows than its rivals. A factor with a level found in one spatial block only is the usual case, and cannot be selected. score_holdout is NA unless select_on = "split", and then the selected set's metric when fitted on the selection half and predicted on the estimation half (\(R^2\) against the selection half's mean, the out-of-sample convention); NA when nothing was selected or the prediction failed. split is NULL or a list with selection and estimation, integer row positions in train_sf as passed; rows the completeness filter above dropped are in neither. params records metric, method, k, tol, seed, auto_range, select_on, n_candidates, estimated_fits, n_scored, rule, se_mult and baseline (its type).

Details

The inner folds must be spatial, and that is the entire point. Nested selection is only worth doing if the inner loop is blocked the same way the outer one is. Random inner folds inside blocked outer folds select variables that look predictive only because nearby points leak between train and test. The outer loop then reports honest-looking numbers for a dishonestly chosen feature set, which is worse than not selecting at all, because the dishonesty is now hidden behind a defensible-looking validation. method therefore defaults to "block_kfold" and logs a loud caution if set to "random_kfold" (a deliberate choice, so it is not raised as an R warning).

Call this inside the fit_fn you pass to cv_spatial(). .cv_fit_one_fold() calls fit_fn(train_sf) on the training slice only, so anything done inside it is automatically nested and leak-free; no extra plumbing is needed. The cost grows fast: a sweep over p candidates costs roughly p^2 / 2 * k model fits, and nesting that inside n outer leave-one-out folds multiplies it by n. max_fits guards against that.

When a variable is accepted

Each candidate set is scored by cross-validation on the same inner folds, and the candidate with the best pooled score is the one considered. Under rule = "se" it is accepted when two things hold: the pooled score improves by more than tol, and the mean of the per-fold improvements (the metric computed in each fold for the set with and without the candidate, and differenced) exceeds se_mult times the standard error of that mean across the folds. This is the one-standard-error idea of Breiman et al. (1984) applied to a step: a gain the folds do not agree on is not evidence that the variable predicts. The fold is the unit because under spatially blocked folds the errors within a block are correlated, so a standard error over rows would understate the noise. With tol = 0 and any gain accepted (the previous default, still available as rule = "tol"), a GWR sweep over one real predictor and six noise candidates added a noise variable in 11 runs of 20; the default rule added one in 4 of 20 and kept the real predictor in all 20. The rule costs power on weak predictors: a second real predictor with a coefficient of 0.3 against 1 was kept in 14 runs of 20, against 18 of 20 when any gain was accepted. With few folds the standard error is itself noisy, so raise k before lowering se_mult. history records each candidate's pooled gain, mean per-fold gain and its standard error, and fold_scores the per-fold scores themselves, so every decision can be checked.

The baseline for the first variable

The first variable is compared with a model that has no predictors, which is recorded as step 0 of history. Which model that is depends on the learner, and baseline$type says which was used:

"null model"

fit_fn(train_sf, character(0)), when the learner can fit it. Step 1 is tested against it like any other step.

"null_fn"

the model null_fn(train_sf) returns, for a learner that cannot fit an empty set but has a natural no-predictor model. Step 1 is tested against it.

"fold mean"

the mean response of each fold's training rows, when neither is available; fit_rf_model refuses an empty predictor set. Here the first variable is provisional: it is added without a test, the sweep continues by the rule, and the finished set is kept only if it beats the fold mean by the same rule; otherwise nothing is selected, and baseline$path holds the set that was reached. The test is at the end of the path, not at step 1, because a forest on a single variable can lose to the mean when two variables together beat it clearly (at a true \(R^2\) of 0.33 the best single-variable forest had RMSE 1.276 against 1.206 for the mean and 1.101 for the pair), so a test at step 1 would select nothing there. The first variable of a kept path then gets a test of its own; see The first variable under a fold-mean baseline.

Without a baseline, as before, at least one variable was always selected: with a forest, in 10 draws of 10 on a response unrelated to every candidate.

The first variable under a fold-mean baseline

The test at the end of the path is of the whole set, so it does not show that the first variable belongs in it: two real predictors and an unrelated candidate that happened to score best alone beat the mean as the two real ones do. A kept path of two or more variables is therefore scored once more without its first variable (one more set, k more fits). That variable is dropped from selected when the set is no better with it by the rule and the rest of the path still beats the fold mean by the rule. baseline$first records the test and baseline$path keeps the set as the sweep reached it, so selected is baseline$path[-1] after a drop. A path of one variable needs no second test: the test against the fold mean was the test of that variable.

This test is the one every later variable passed, an improvement of the set by the rule, and it has the same limit. In 20 forest sweeps at a true \(R^2\) of 0.33, with two real predictors and three unrelated candidates, the path began with an unrelated candidate in 3: it was dropped in 2 and kept in 1, where the forest scored better with it than without (Selection with a random forest says why it can). At a true \(R^2\) of 0.15, 9 selections of 20 were kept, 3 of them began with an unrelated candidate, and all 3 kept it for that reason. So in a selection of two or more variables from a learner that falls back to the fold mean, selected[1] has been shown to improve the set, not to predict on its own. The test also costs power on a weak first predictor, as the rule does at every step: with one real predictor of coefficient 0.3 and five unrelated candidates, a linear learner that refuses the empty set kept the real predictor in 77 sweeps of 100, against 80 before this test existed and 77 for the same learner fitting its own null model (in the 3 sweeps that differ it was the first variable, its gain was within one standard error, and the learner with a null model selected nothing). When the set is no better with the first variable but the rest of the path does not beat the fold mean by the rule either, the two cannot be told apart: the set is kept whole, a caution is logged, and baseline$first$note says the variable is unproven. A learner that fits its own null model gets no such test: its first variable passed one at step 1.

The baseline for a GWR

For a GWR the fold mean is a weak baseline, because every GWR carries a local intercept and beats a global mean on any smooth response whatever its predictors are: on a smooth response unrelated to six candidates, a GWR sweep against the fold mean selected one of them in 20 runs of 20. Each of those paths had one variable, which the test of the first variable above does not reach. The comparison that matters there is with the kernel-weighted local mean at the same bandwidth, a GWR with a local intercept and no predictors: against it the same sweeps selected a variable in 4 runs of 20. fit_gwr_model fits that model when its predictor_vars is character(0), so a fit_fn that hands its variables to fit_gwr_model() gets it as the null model, and the first variable is tested against it at step 1 (baseline$type is "null model"). Give such a fit_fn a fixed bandwidth, so that every set is fitted under the kernel the baseline has; with bandwidth = NULL each set, the empty one included, searches for its own. A fit_fn that refuses an empty set falls back to the fold mean, and the sweep logs a caution: read a GWR selection of one variable made that way as unproven, or supply the local mean as null_fn, as the second half of the example at the end of this page does for a learner written by hand.

predict() on a GWR warns about held-out locations it cannot estimate and about those beyond the reach of a fold's fit (classes "spatialkit_gwr_not_estimable" and "spatialkit_gwr_extrapolation"; see predict.gwr_fit). The sweep raises each once, under this function's name, with the totals over the candidate sets it scored; every set is predicted on the same rows, so a location can be counted once per set.

Selection with a random forest

A forest confounds selection with tuning. Adding a predictor that carries no signal still changes how the trees split, and with ranger's default node size that regularises the forest: in one test the cross-validated RMSE was 1.458 with the real predictor alone, 1.340 with a noise variable added, and 1.341 with the real predictor alone and min_node_size = 20. The noise variable bought what tuning the node size buys. That gain is real, so no acceptance rule refuses it: with one real predictor and six noise candidates a forest sweep kept the real one in 20 runs of 20 and added 1.35 noise variables per run under the default rule (2.4 per run, over 10 runs, when any gain was accepted). Setting the node size in fit_fn reduces this without removing it (0.8 per run at min_node_size = 20). So a variable in a forest selection may be there as a tuning effect wherever in the order it was added: later additions with small gains are the usual case, and the first variable is another, because a forest sweep starts from the fold mean and its first variable is tested as an addition to the others (see The first variable under a fold-mean baseline). Compare the selected set with a tuned forest on the variables you have other reasons to believe in:


fit_fn <- function(train_sf, vars)
  fit_rf_model(train_sf, "z", vars, min_node_size = 20)

On a response unrelated to every candidate the same sweeps selected nothing in 20 runs of 20 (19 of 20 with the larger node size).

The score is not a performance estimate

$score is the cross-validated metric of the winning set at the final step: the best of every candidate set the sweep scored. That is the number the selection optimised, and a number optimised over many candidates is optimistically biased by construction: Cawley and Talbot (2010) show the bias can exceed the genuine differences between the models being compared. Quote it as the selection criterion, not as the performance of the selected model. An honest performance estimate needs data the selection never saw. Two ways to get one: run this function inside the fit_fn of cv_spatial(), so the outer folds score a model whose predictors were chosen on the inner ones alone; or pass select_on = "split", which selects on one spatial half of train_sf and returns the selected set's score on the other as score_holdout.

References

Breiman, L., Friedman, J. H., Olshen, R. A. and Stone, C. J. (1984). Classification and Regression Trees. Wadsworth.

Cawley, G. C. and Talbot, N. L. C. (2010). On over-fitting in model selection and subsequent selection bias in performance evaluation. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 11, 2079–2107. https://jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html

See also

Other cross-validation: area_of_applicability(), cv_bayes(), cv_block_size_sweep(), cv_gwr(), cv_rf(), cv_spatial(), estimate_sac_range(), fold_separation(), gwr_model_selection(), make_folds(), sac_nugget()

Examples

if (requireNamespace("sp", quietly = TRUE)) {
  library(sf)
  set.seed(1)
  n <- 120
  pts <- st_as_sf(
    data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(n, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(n, 0, 1000),
               a = rnorm(n), b = rnorm(n), noise = rnorm(n)),
    coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632
  )
  pts$resp <- 3 * pts$a + 2 * pts$b + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3)

  # The learner: a GWR with an adaptive bisquare kernel reaching the 30th
  # nearest training point.  With no variables it is the kernel-weighted
  # local mean, which is the baseline: a GWR's local intercept beats a
  # global mean on any smooth response, so the first variable has to beat
  # the local mean under the same kernel.
  fit_fn <- function(tr, vars) fit_gwr_model(tr, "resp", vars, bandwidth = 30)
  sel <- select_features_forward(pts, "resp", c("a", "b", "noise"), fit_fn,
                                 k = 3, quiet = TRUE)
  sel$selected
  sel$baseline$type        # "null model": step 1 was tested against it
  sel$history[sel$history$step <= 1, c("step", "variable", "score", "gain")]

  # A learner that cannot fit an empty set takes its no-predictor model
  # through `null_fn`.  Here the same local mean, written as a spatial_fit
  # of its own with a predict() method, for a learner that insists on a
  # variable.  Without `null_fn` that sweep would start from the mean of
  # each training fold.
  needs_one <- function(tr, vars) {
    if (!length(vars)) stop("this learner needs a predictor")
    fit_gwr_model(tr, "resp", vars, bandwidth = 30)
  }
  local_mean <- function(tr, bandwidth = 30) {
    new_spatial_fit("local_mean_fit",
                    engine = list(xy = st_coordinates(tr), y = tr$resp,
                                  bandwidth = bandwidth),
                    formula = resp ~ 1, response_var = "resp",
                    predictor_vars = character(0), data_sf = tr)
  }
  predict.local_mean_fit <- function(object, newdata = NULL, ...) {
    e  <- object$engine
    at <- if (is.null(newdata)) e$xy else st_coordinates(newdata)
    vapply(seq_len(nrow(at)), function(i) {
      d <- sqrt((e$xy[, 1] - at[i, 1])^2 + (e$xy[, 2] - at[i, 2])^2)
      h <- sort(d)[min(e$bandwidth, length(d))]  # the kernel's reach here
      w <- ifelse(d > h, 0, (1 - d^2 / h^2)^2)   # bisquare weights
      sum(w * e$y) / sum(w)
    }, numeric(1))
  }
  registerS3method("predict", "local_mean_fit", predict.local_mean_fit)
  sel2 <- select_features_forward(pts, "resp", c("a", "b", "noise"), needs_one,
                                  k = 3, quiet = TRUE, null_fn = local_mean)
  sel2$baseline$type       # "null_fn"
  all.equal(sel2$baseline$score, sel$baseline$score)  # the same baseline
}
#> [1] TRUE
